q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP AS ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) AS ITEMPRICE, ITM AS ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP AS ITP, ITM AS ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP AS ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) AS ITEMPRICE, ITM AS ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP AS ITP, ITM AS ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
counterexample: INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 1500); INSERT INTO ITP (ITEMNO, NP) VALUES (1, 2000); INSERT INTO ITM (ITEMNO, TYPE) VALUES (1, 'A');
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent. Q1 first selects distinct ITEMNO and NP from ITP where NP > 1000, then joins with ITM on ITEMNO. Q2 directly selects distinct NP, TYPE, and ITEMNO from ITP and ITM with NP > 1000 and ITEMNO join condition. The difference arises because Q1's subquery removes duplicates before the join, while Q2 applies DISTINCT after the join. This can lead to different results when multiple rows in ITP have the same ITEMNO and NP > 1000.
counterexample_dsp: A scenario where ITP has multiple rows with the same ITEMNO and NP > 1000. Q1 will return one row per ITEMNO (distinct), while Q2 will return one row per (ITEMNO, NP) combination, potentially more rows if NP varies for same ITEMNO.
